prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks and their development to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: Optical lattice clocks pair a single conceptual step, Katori's magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, with an experimental programme, led by Ye, that took fractional uncertainty to the 1e-18 level and below. The result is checkable and does not depend on interpretation: independent national laboratories reproduce it and compare clocks, and it supports tests of relativity and of constant variation, relativistic geodesy and the pending redefinition of the SI second. The credited pair is exactly two names, which is a clean attribution with no forced exclusion, unlike the three other leading candidates. As a theorist who computes polarizabilities, multipole and blackbody shifts, I can say that the control of these atomic-structure effects is what made the 1e-18 regime reachable, so the achievement is physical and not merely technical. It is also seven-way supported in the opening ballots, with two first places and five top-three rankings.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier recognition of precision frequency metrology (the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for quantum control of single ions), and the possibility that the committee may prefer to wait until the second is actually redefined. There is also a fair worry that a two-name prize leaves out other lattice-clock pioneers (Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat and others) and that the measurement-science subfield is being favoured over a conceptual change in condensed-matter physics such as topological insulators, which has more first-place votes.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked B034 third and noted that Ye's frequency-comb work overlaps with the 2005 prize and that other lattice-clock pioneers and the unfinished redefinition of the second could complicate credit.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously but think it is narrower than it appears. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a tool for optical frequency measurement; the lattice clock is a distinct scheme, the magic-wavelength trap, which removes the Doppler and recoil limits for many atoms at once and has moved the clock accuracy by orders of magnitude. Ye's credited contribution here is the realisation and systematic-shift control of the strontium clock, not the comb. I agree that the redefinition is pending, but the scientific discovery does not hinge on it, and waiting for an administrative decision would make the prize depend on metrology bodies instead of on what was demonstrated.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B028 first with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, arguing that theory, the HgTe experiment and the 3D ARPES identification form a clear chain, and that the 2016 prize concerned a related but distinct topic.
responses.response: I agree that topological insulators are a central, original and now mature idea, and I ranked B028 third, so I would be content to see it awarded. My disagreement is about the configuration: your trio drops Mele, whom six of seven openings, including mine, credit as a co-originator of the Z2 invariant, and keeping him means dropping Hasan, so the 2D versus 3D split remains unresolved. The missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang theory credit is a second problem. I also think the 2016 prize overlap is more significant than you suggest, since it already honoured topological phases of matter in the Thouless-Haldane-Kosterlitz sense. A prize with a clean two-name attribution and no overlap seems to me more defensible this year, with B028 as the first alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B046 first, calling the magic-angle prediction followed by the 2018 experiments a rare case where electronic-structure theory guided a field-defining experiment, while leaving the third name between Andrei and Bistritzer.
responses.response: The theory-then-experiment arc is a real strength and I put B046 second. But the unresolved third slot you identify is serious: four credited people, a contested Andrei versus Bistritzer priority, and Cao, the first author of the 2018 papers, absent from the names. Add the still-debated pairing mechanism and only about eight years since the key experiments, and I regard this as less ready than the clock, whose claims are settled and independently reproduced. I would not oppose it as an alternative, but I would not pick it first.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B034 first, calling Katori and Ye the two decisive strands with a clean two-person credit, and flagged his own personal link to Ye's Hall-lab environment.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and with the maturity argument. Where I would add something is on his disclosure: it is wise to record it, since it bears on whether Kroll should take part in any final decision on this very candidate. I would not want my support for B034 to rest on his view alone, since the case should stand on the independent agreement of the clocks and on the atomic-structure physics behind them, which is separate from any laboratory affiliation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as too close to the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the SI second before recognising the clock.
I have not independently verified the current best uncertainty figures or the priority of other lattice-clock groups.
Whether a two-name prize on B034 can command more support than a topological-insulators prize on B028, where the allocation of three names is contested but the opening support is broader.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred B034 candidates Katori and Ye: my documented collaborations are with L'Huillier and the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, Schuch, Dahlstrom, Argenti and Indelicato, none of whom are credited here. I work in theoretical atomic physics and attosecond science, so a general subject proximity to precision atomic structure exists, but this is not a personal or institutional connection. None of the credited names in my alternatives B028 and B046 are among my listed collaborators.
